title: The Kestrel Over the Lost Thing
creature: A kestrel who hangs still above whatever is missing
summary: She held her place over the same field for four days before anyone thought to go and look.

chapters.title: Hanging
chapters.text: A kestrel hunting hangs in the air. That is the thing about them that everybody notices first and that Tomás's father had explained to him when he was about six, on the way to somewhere, in the way of a man filling four minutes in a car. She faces the wind and she flies forward at exactly the speed the wind is coming at her, and the two cancel, and she stops. Not gliding, not soaring — actively flying, hard, and staying in one place. Her head does not move at all. The body shifts and the wings work and the tail spreads and closes, and the head hangs there in the air as though it has been nailed to a point in the sky. Then she moves a dozen metres and does it again over the next patch. That is the whole method. She holds still, she looks, she moves on. A field is searched in about forty minutes. The reason she has to hang there, his father had said, is that she is looking for something that is trying not to be seen, in grass, from twelve metres up, and the only way to do that is to hold your eye absolutely still over one patch until the patch gives something away. Everything about the bird is built round that one requirement. The wings are doing enormous work. The tail is doing continuous small corrections. The head is doing nothing at all, and the doing-nothing is the entire point of the rest of it. Tomás had thought that was the best thing he had ever heard and had told several people at school, who had not agreed. Which is why, when she stopped moving on, Tomás noticed. He was thirteen and he went past the Vasco field twice a day on the bike, and on the Monday she was hanging over the near corner, and on the Tuesday she was hanging over the near corner, and on the Wednesday morning she was over the near corner and he stopped the bike and put his foot down and watched her for twelve minutes. She was working. That was what was wrong. She was not perched somewhere with a good view, saving her energy, which is what a bird does when it is not hunting. She was hovering — which is expensive, which is the most expensive thing a small bird can do — over one patch of ground about the size of a garage, for a third day. There was nothing there. He could see the whole of it from the road. Stubble, a bit of thistle, the concrete pad where a shed had been.

chapters.title: What the Bird Was Doing
chapters.text: He asked at home and got the answer people give. His mother said there was probably a nest of something. His father said the same and added that the field had been left three years and was full of voles and that a bird over a field was not news. His sister, who was nineteen and studying something with animals in it and who was therefore insufferable that year, said that kestrels absolutely do repeat productive patches and that Tomás had discovered nothing. She was right, as it happens, about the general case. That is what makes the argument worth reporting. Kestrels do repeat productive patches. They will work a good verge for weeks. Everything his sister said at that table was correct as a statement about kestrels, and it was delivered with the total confidence of somebody in the second year of a degree, and it was very nearly the reason Tomás dropped the whole thing. He has thought about that more than about any other part of it. She had better information than he did. She had actual training. And what she did with the better information was use it to explain away an observation she had not made, about a field she had not looked at, because the observation had come from her thirteen-year-old brother. He went back on the Thursday mostly out of spite. He would like to be able to claim a better reason and there was not one. He went back on the Thursday. She was there. Same corner. Same height, which he had started estimating and had settled at about twelve metres. He watched her for half an hour this time and counted. He had brought a watch and a notebook, having decided overnight to be serious about it, and he sat on the verge with the bike laid over in the grass and did the thing properly. In thirty-one minutes she came down twice — properly stooped, dropped feet-first into the stubble — and came up twice with nothing, and went straight back to the same place and hung again. That was the part that undid the vole theory. A kestrel that misses moves. It is not sentimental about a patch. Two misses in half an hour on the fourth day and she was still there. He worked out the rest of it on the way home, standing on the pedals up the hill. Hovering costs. He did not have the number, but he did not need the number; he had watched her do it for thirty-one minutes without a break longer than a few seconds, and anything that looks that much like hard work is hard work. A bird does not spend four days doing the most expensive thing it can do over a patch of stubble the size of a garage because it is fond of the view. Either there was something there worth four days, or she was broken. And she was plainly not broken. She was hovering beautifully — better, if anything, than the ones he saw over the motorway, holding position in a crosswind that was pushing the thistles about. So there was something there. He had been looking at the wrong part of the field for three days. He had been looking at the grass, because the grass is where a vole is. He had not once looked at the concrete. He said this at dinner, with numbers, and his sister said that was actually interesting, in the tone of somebody surprised to be saying it. His father put his fork down. "Fourth day." "Fourth." "Which corner?" "The one by the road. Where the shed was." His father looked at the table for a moment and then said, "Ask Old Vasco."

chapters.title: Old Vasco
chapters.text: Vasco was ninety-one and lived in the house at the top of the lane and had not farmed the field in a dozen years. He was hard to talk to. Not unfriendly — he simply took a long time to arrive at a conversation, and if you filled the silences he would let you, and then you would have said everything and he would have said nothing. Tomás had been coached on this by his father in the car and did the difficult thing, which was to state the situation in four sentences and then stop talking. Vasco sat in his chair for what felt like a year. Then he said: "By the concrete." "Yes." "How high." "About twelve metres. Same place, four days." Vasco nodded slowly, twice, and then said something that Tomás did not follow at all, which was: "Then it's not a vole, and I'm too old to go down there, and you'd better take a spade." He would not explain further. Tomás asked twice. What he said, on the way out, at the door, in the tone of a man deciding to give away one thing and not two, was this: "My father used to say you don't look for a lost thing. You look for what's paying attention to it."

chapters.title: What Was Under the Concrete
chapters.text: It was not treasure and Tomás would like that stated at the top, because when he tells this story people always lean forward at exactly this point and he always has to take it away from them. It was a dog. The concrete pad was the floor of a shed that had come down in about 2009, and along the road edge of it the slab had cracked and settled and left a gap about the width of a fist between the concrete and the earth, and under the slab there was a void perhaps a metre across where the ground had washed out. A dog had gone in after something and could not get back out. She had been in there four days. Four days. Tomás did that arithmetic standing on the concrete with his father's jacket in his hands and it is the only part of the whole business that still gets him. She had been under there on the Monday, when he cycled past twice and looked at a bird. She had been under there on the Tuesday and the Wednesday, when he stopped and watched for twelve minutes and decided there was nothing in that corner. She had been under there on the Thursday morning while he sat on the verge with a notebook and a watch, being pleased with himself about method. She was a small brown mongrel with a collar and no tag and she was extremely thin and completely silent, which was why nobody walking the road had heard a thing — she had gone past barking days ago and was doing the other thing, the quiet thing, that animals do at the end of it. It took Tomás, his father, and a neighbour with a crowbar about ninety minutes to get the slab up enough to reach in. The first twenty minutes were spent establishing that there was anything there at all, because the gap was a fist wide and dark and Tomás's father would not let him put his arm in it. They got a torch on it. Then they got a longer torch on it. Then Tomás lay flat on the concrete with his cheek against it and his eye at the gap for about a minute, in silence, with the two men standing over him, and said, in a voice he did not entirely recognise, "There's a dog." After that it was a matter of levers and swearing. The slab was thicker than it looked and had reinforcing in it, and they could not lift it, and in the end they did not lift it — they broke the corner off it with a sledge, in stages, going carefully because nobody knew exactly where under there she was. She did not make a sound the entire time. Not when the sledge went in. Not when the corner came away and the light got to her. Tomás's father put his jacket over her and got her out with both hands, and she weighed, he said afterwards, about as much as a bag of sugar, and she was still trying to wag. The kestrel was overhead for the first half of it and then was not, and Tomás did not see her go. He has thought about the bird every so often for twenty years and he has arrived at a position that satisfies him about eighty per cent of the time. There were flies. There must have been flies, and there were probably beetles, and there was something dying in a hole in a field, and a kestrel is an opportunist and will take an insect and will absolutely notice a smell and a movement and a change in a patch of ground. That is almost certainly all it was. She was not standing guard. She was not signalling. She was a small falcon economically monitoring an anomaly, for four days, at considerable metabolic cost, because there was something in that corner and she had noticed and she is built to notice. Which is, when he says it out loud, not actually a smaller thing than the version people want. The dog belonged to a family in Almeirim who had lost her from a car five days earlier and had put up posters in the wrong town. She lived another nine years. Tomás is thirty-three. He does not have a job that has anything to do with birds. But he has never in his life been able to walk past a hovering kestrel without stopping, and he has twice made himself late for things by standing in a road counting the minutes she stays in one place, and once — only once, in a lay-by on the way to Beja in 2019, over a drainage ditch — it was four days again, and he went and looked, and there was nothing there at all, and he sat back in the car feeling foolish and then, on the whole, not.
